passage:
Joseph, sit with your Ammachi Elizabeth a minute. You remind me of your uncle Benny at fifteen. I'm his mother, so I saw all of it.
The week of the school play, one pimple came up on his nose, and he was certain the whole hall would stare at nothing else. He wore a cap to dinner. Then a girl he liked stopped talking to him, and he said, "Amma, you can't understand. No one has ever felt like this." I didn't argue. He wasn't ready to hear it.
That summer he went to a youth camp in Munnar. He came back talking about a boy from Kochi who had lost his best friend, and a girl who hated her braces. "Everyone's got something," he said, surprised.
The cap went back in the cupboard.

qa.q: Where did Benny go that summer?
qa.a: To a youth camp in Munnar.

qa.q: Why was Benny so sure the whole hall would stare at his pimple?
qa.a: At fifteen he felt as if he were always on a stage with everyone watching, so one small spot seemed huge to everyone else too.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make when Benny said nobody could understand, and why?
qa.a: She didn't argue, because he wasn't ready to hear it; meeting other young people at camp showed him instead.

qa.q: What might Joseph take from hearing about Benny?
qa.a: Joseph might feel less alone, seeing that an uncle who seems settled now once felt nobody in the world could understand him.

grounding: A grandmother tells how her teenage son felt watched and uniquely hurt until meeting others at a camp softened it.

passage:
Rain had soaked Nagpur since morning, and the sole of Hrithik's left shoe had started to flap. New shoes would have to wait until his father's pay came at the end of the month.
On the walk to tuition, every squelch felt like an announcement. Hrithik was sure the girls at the bus stop were laughing at his feet. Nobody in the history of Class 9 had ever been this embarrassed, he decided.
At tuition he tucked both feet under the bench. Pankaj, sitting beside him, leaned over. "Yours too?" He lifted his own foot: a strip of tape wound round the toe. Across the room, the new boy from Wardha had plastic bags inside his sandals against the wet.
Hrithik looked at the three pairs of feet and, for the first time that day, laughed.

qa.q: What did Pankaj have round the toe of his shoe?
qa.a: A strip of tape.

qa.q: Why was Hrithik sure the girls at the bus stop were laughing at his feet?
qa.a: Ashamed of the flapping sole, Hrithik felt as if every eye was on him, so any laughter nearby seemed to be about his shoe 😰

qa.q: What turning point eased Hrithik's embarrassment?
qa.a: Seeing Pankaj's taped shoe and the plastic bags in the new boy's sandals showed him he wasn't the only one.

qa.q: Why might Pankaj have chosen to show his own taped shoe?
qa.a: Pankaj may have noticed Hrithik hiding his feet and wanted him to know it happens to others too, easing the shame without a speech.

grounding: A fourteen-year-old boy on a rainy day feels that everyone is watching his broken shoe and that no one has felt this before, until he sees classmates in the same spot.

passage:
Vaibhav, sixteen, kept his poems in a locked folder on his phone. Nobody, he was sure, had ever felt as alone in a crowded Bengaluru flat as he did. When his older sister Yamini dragged him to a Sunday open mic in a Jayanagar bookshop, he sat at the back, certain every head would turn if he so much as coughed.
A college girl read a poem about feeling invisible at her own dinner table. A retired bank clerk read about missing his village. Vaibhav's lips moved along with some of the lines.
In the auto home, he said, "That clerk uncle wrote my poem. Forty years before me."
Yamini kept her eyes on the traffic. "Next month, you read one."

qa.q: Where was the Sunday open mic held?
qa.a: In a Jayanagar bookshop.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav sit at the back, sure every head would turn?
qa.a: At sixteen Vaibhav felt lonely and self-conscious, as if constantly watched, so even a cough seemed like something the whole room would notice.

qa.q: What choice of Yamini's helped soften Vaibhav's sense that nobody felt like him?
qa.a: Taking him to the open mic, where strangers described his own feelings, rather than simply telling him he wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might the retired clerk feel if he knew Vaibhav recognised his poem?
qa.a: He would likely be moved that a teenager heard his own feeling in it, forty years apart 🙂

grounding: A sixteen-year-old boy who feels uniquely alone and watched begins to soften when he hears strangers voice the same feelings.

passage: "Amma, I'm not going to school tomorrow." "Why, Kartik?" "Everyone saw me drop the trophy on stage. Everyone. They're all talking about it." "Everyone?" "The whole school, Amma. Nobody has ever been this humiliated. Ever." "Aparna, didn't you fall off the stage in Class 9?" "Into the flower pots. In a sari. In front of the chief guest." "Akka, that's different. It's not the same for me." "Kartik, how many people mentioned it today?" "...Two. But they were all thinking it." "Or thinking about their own lunch." "You don't understand." Aparna ruffled his hair. "Maybe not. But I still remember the flower pots, and nobody else does." Kartik almost smiled. "The chief guest, really?" "Front row." Rukmini, their Amma, put a plate of murukku between them.

qa.q: How many people mentioned the trophy to Kartik that day?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: Why is Kartik so sure the whole school is talking about him?
qa.a: He feels that everyone is watching him and that his embarrassment is unlike anyone else's, so two comments seem like the whole school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation for Kartik?
qa.a: Aparna's flower-pot story and her saying nobody else remembers it, which made him almost smile and see others have felt this too.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel sharing her own embarrassing fall with her brother?
qa.a: She seems warm and a little amused, willing to laugh at herself so that he feels less alone.

grounding: A teenage boy feels his embarrassment is unique and that everyone is watching him, and his sister's story begins to soften that.

passage: Last year, when my best friend Bhavna moved to Delhi, I was sure nobody in the history of the world had felt what I felt. I wrote it in a notebook: "No one understands. No one could." Walking into school, I felt every face turn to check whether I looked sad. I even changed how I walked. Then in December I went to an inter-school science camp in Mysuru. On the second night, sitting on the hostel steps, a boy from Hubli said his closest friend had moved to Dubai, and he'd felt everyone staring at him for weeks. Another boy nodded. I just sat there. My exact feeling, in somebody else's mouth. I'm Kunal, and I still have that notebook. It reads a little differently now. Amma calls it her son's tragic-poet phase.

qa.q: Where was the inter-school science camp?
qa.a: In Mysuru.

qa.q: Why did Kunal change how he walked into school?
qa.a: He felt everyone was watching him to see if he looked sad, and believed his pain was unlike anyone else's.

qa.q: What turning point softened Kunal's belief that no one could understand?
qa.a: Hearing a boy from Hubli describe the same feeling on the hostel steps, which showed others had felt it too.

qa.q: How might the boy from Hubli have felt when Kunal sat there listening?
qa.a: He may have felt less alone too, sharing something private and finding that others nodded in recognition.

grounding: A teenage boy looks back on feeling that nobody had ever felt his loss and everyone was watching him, until meeting others softened it.

passage: At the morning assembly in the Nagpur school, Deepak stood in the fourth row with a new haircut his uncle had given him the night before. It was too short at the back. He was certain every single person was staring at it. He kept his hand on his neck through the whole prayer. At lunch he went to the counsellor's room instead of the canteen. "Nobody has ever looked this bad," he told Pankaj sir. "Nobody understands." Pankaj sir nodded seriously. "That feeling is real. Can I ask you something? Can you remember what anyone else's hair looked like today?" Deepak thought. He couldn't. Not one person. That afternoon, in the peer group session, two other boys admitted they had hidden in the library after bad haircuts too. Deepak laughed for the first time that day.

qa.q: Where did Deepak go at lunch instead of the canteen?
qa.a: To the counsellor's room.

qa.q: Why was Deepak sure everyone was staring at his haircut?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and very self-conscious, so it seemed that everyone must be watching him as closely as he was watching himself.

qa.q: What did Pankaj sir's question do well?
qa.a: Asking whether Deepak remembered anyone else's hair gently showed him that others weren't watching him as closely as he feared, without dismissing his feeling.

qa.q: How might the two other boys in the peer session feel sharing their own haircut stories?
qa.a: They might feel relieved and a little sheepish, glad to learn they weren't the only ones.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling that everyone is watching him and nobody has felt this before, and the feeling softening as he hears others.

passage:
Subject: nobody gets it

Yogesh bhaiya,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. My whole friend group has shifted. Aman and Vikram sit with the football boys now, and I'm just there, eating my lunch alone like a character in a sad film. I know you're going to say everyone goes through this. But honestly, nobody has felt what I'm feeling. It's different for me. When I walk into class, I swear everyone looks up and thinks, there's the guy with no friends.

Weird thing, though. At robotics club on Thursday, a class-twelve senior told me the same happened to him in class nine. He said it lasted a few months, then he found the robotics lot.

So maybe not nobody. Did it happen to you too? You never said.

Sahil

qa.q: Where did Sahil meet the class-twelve senior?
qa.a: At robotics club on Thursday.

qa.q: Why does Sahil believe nobody has felt this before?
qa.a: Sahil feels lonely and hurt, and in that pain the experience seems completely unique, as if everyone is looking and judging.

qa.q: What could Sahil do to keep the feeling softening?
qa.a: Sahil could keep going to the robotics club and talk to people like the senior, who have been through something similar.

qa.q: How might Yogesh bhaiya feel reading this email?
qa.a: He would likely feel touched that Sahil trusted him, and want to share his own story to show Sahil isn't alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling the experience is unique and everyone is watching, and the feeling starting to soften after meeting someone older.

passage: Jyoti, you asked for the most embarrassing thing that happened to Rafiq at fourteen, so here it is. Annual day, the school stage. I was playing a tree in the drama. A tree! I walked on and tripped over a cable and fell flat. Everyone laughed. For weeks after, I was sure the whole school remembered. Every time someone laughed in a corridor, I thought, that's about me. I truly believed nobody in history had been this humiliated. Then, at a drama camp the next summer, we played a game where everyone told their worst stage moment. One girl had forgotten every line. A boy had thrown up. Nobody remembered my fall except me. That was the first time I realised the audience I imagined was mostly in my own head.

qa.q: What role was Rafiq playing in the drama?
qa.a: A tree.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq think every corridor laugh was about the fall?
qa.a: Rafiq felt deeply humiliated and self-conscious, so it seemed the whole school was watching and remembering, even though they weren't.

qa.q: What made the drama camp game helpful, and how could a school use something like it?
qa.a: Hearing others share worse moments showed Rafiq that nobody was alone in this; a school club could run the same kind of story circle.

qa.q: How might the girl who forgot every line have felt hearing Rafiq's story?
qa.a: That girl might have felt relieved and less alone, seeing that others had embarrassing moments too.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing the whole school was watching and no one had felt such embarrassment, and the feeling softening at a camp full of new people.

passage:
Monday. Naveen, fifteen, got a haircut that went wrong. He was sure the whole school would stare. He wore a cap all day and kept his head down. At home he told his mother Madhuri, "Nobody has ever looked this stupid."

Wednesday. He took the cap off in class. Two friends noticed; one said, "Nice." Nobody else looked.

Saturday. At his cousin's birthday, three other boys had haircuts even worse than his. Naveen laughed. "I thought I was the only one."

Madhuri smiled. "Most people are busy worrying about themselves."

Naveen went home lighter, feeling a little silly about the cap.

qa.q: How many other boys at the birthday had worse haircuts?
qa.a: Three other boys.

qa.q: Why did Naveen wear a cap all day on Monday?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and sure the whole school would stare, as if all eyes were on him.

qa.q: What did Madhuri say that might help Naveen next time?
qa.a: That most people are busy worrying about themselves, so he doesn't need to feel everyone is watching.

qa.q: How might Naveen's friends see his haircut?
qa.a: They barely noticed; one even said "Nice," so they were much less focused on it than Naveen.

grounding: A teenager feels everyone is watching his bad haircut and that nobody has felt this before, until meeting others softens it.

passage:
Siddharth, you think nobody in the world has ever felt what you're feeling about this girl? Let your Deepak chacha tell you something.

When I was sixteen, I fell hard for a girl in my tuition class. I thought my feelings were deeper than anyone's ever. I wrote poems. I thought the whole tuition class was watching me blush every day.

Then one evening, my father found a poem. He didn't laugh. He told me about the girl he liked at sixteen. He'd written poems too.

I was stunned. My father! Slowly, as I talked to more people, I realised everyone had felt something like this. It didn't make my feelings smaller. It made me less lonely.

qa.q: What did Deepak's father find?
qa.a: A poem.

qa.q: How did young Deepak feel when his father told his own story?
qa.a: He felt stunned, then less lonely, realising his feelings weren't unique.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Deepak saw his feelings?
qa.a: His father sharing his own sixteen-year-old poems made Deepak see others had felt the same.

qa.q: How might Deepak's father have felt finding the poem?
qa.a: His father probably felt tender and nostalgic, remembering his own first crush.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling as a teenager that nobody had felt what he felt, until his father's story softened it.

passage:
The debate final was in two hours, and Sachin, sixteen, couldn't stop checking his reflection. There was a pimple on his chin. He was sure every judge would see nothing else.

"Everyone's going to stare at it," he told his teammate Naveen.

"What?"

"This!" Sachin pointed at his chin.

Naveen squinted. "I can barely see it. Honestly, I'm worried about my own speech."

Sachin stopped. Naveen was worried too?

On stage, the lights were bright and his voice shook at first. But nobody looked at his chin. The judges wrote notes. The audience clapped. Afterwards, three people complimented his argument. Nobody mentioned the pimple.

qa.q: How long before the debate final did Sachin check his reflection?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: Why was Sachin sure everyone would stare at his chin?
qa.a: He felt anxious and self-conscious, as if everyone was watching him closely.

qa.q: What helped Sachin see things differently?
qa.a: Naveen said he could barely see it and was worried about his own speech, showing others had their own worries.

qa.q: How did the audience actually react to Sachin?
qa.a: They clapped and three people complimented his argument; nobody mentioned the pimple.

grounding: Under pressure, a teenager feels everyone is watching him and his flaw, until he sees others are busy with their own worries.

passage: Naveen spent twenty minutes at the bathroom mirror of their Chennai flat, staring at the pimple on his chin. At the school annual day, he was sure every head in the hall turned toward it. He kept his hand over his face during the prize list. Afterwards his friend Harish slapped his back. "Why were you hiding? Nobody's looking at you, machan. They're looking at their own phones." Naveen didn't believe him. That night he typed in his notes: "No one understands. Nobody has ever felt this stupid." The next morning, his older cousin, visiting from Bengaluru, laughed at breakfast about her own "volcano chin" at sixteen. Naveen looked up, surprised.

qa.q: Why did Naveen keep his hand over his face during the prize list?

qa.q: What could help Naveen feel less alone?

grounding: A teenager feels everyone is watching him and that no one has ever felt this way, until a cousin shares the same experience.

passage: When I was fifteen, I was sure I was the only person in history who felt like a stranger in my own family. I also believed that every time I walked into the gurdwara, the whole sangat noticed my new haircut and judged me. I wrote long, dramatic poems about it. Then I went to a summer theatre camp, and on the second night Rajni, the camp leader, asked us to write one secret feeling on a slip of paper. She read them out without names. Five slips said, "Nobody at home understands me." Three said, "I feel like everyone is watching me." I sat there stunned. My poem was still mine, but I wasn't alone in it. I'm Baljeet, and I still write, just less dramatically.

qa.q: How many slips said "Nobody at home understands me"?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the slips were read out?
qa.a: Stunned, and then less alone: the feeling was still personal, but others shared it.

qa.q: What made the difference for Baljeet?
qa.a: Meeting other teenagers at camp and hearing their anonymous feelings, which showed the experience was common.

qa.q: What might Rajni have hoped the slip exercise would do?
qa.a: Help the campers see they weren't alone, gently widening their view without dismissing their feelings.

grounding: A teenager believed those feelings were unique and that everyone was watching, until meeting others at camp showed otherwise.

passage:
Camp log, monsoon nature camp, days one to four.
Day one: Omkar kept his hood up at every meal. When I asked, he said, "Nobody here gets what it's like to switch schools three times. And everyone stared when I slipped on the path." Nobody had; most were busy scraping mud off their own shoes.
Day three: during the leech check, Chandrika mentioned she had moved cities twice. Omkar looked at her as if she had spoken a secret language. They talked until the lamps went off.
Day four: he slipped again and laughed, and so did two others. I paired him with Chandrika for the river walk and told him that half this group arrived as newcomers. "Seriously? Half?" he said.
Next: I will remind everyone about the group chat so they keep in touch after camp.

qa.q: What did Chandrika mention during the leech check?
qa.a: She mentioned that she had moved cities twice.

qa.q: Why did Omkar believe everyone stared when he slipped?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious and alone, so his own embarrassment seemed like the centre of everyone's attention, even though most were busy with their own muddy shoes.

qa.q: What did the camp leader do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: Pairing Omkar with Chandrika and telling him many were newcomers widened his view; keeping the group in touch after camp can help that last.

qa.q: How is Chandrika affected when Omkar finds out she shares his experience?
qa.a: She likely feels connected too, since they talked until the lamps went off; her small remark helped someone else feel less alone.

grounding: A teenager feels nobody shares his experience and that all eyes are on him, and the feeling softens as he meets others with similar stories.
